continuity_scope: A bounded, tradition-level orientation pass for the broader Sanskrit Mahābhārata tradition, not a replacement text or a universal canon. Primary textual orientation is limited to the Adi Parva frame (Ugraśravas Sauti and Śaunaka) and two Vana Parva embedded narratives (Nala–Damayantī and Sāvitrī–Satyavān), using Kisari Mohan Ganguli’s public-domain English translation as an accessible, non-critical translation witness. Oxford Academic scholarship establishes that the Mahābhārata is best approached as a plurality of oral, textual, and performative traditions. This pass is distinct from SRC-277 BORI Critical Edition and SRC-278 Bhagavad Gītā; it neither transfers their claims nor merges their character records.
work_or_witnesses: Mahābhārata, Adi Parva, Section I and Pauloma Parva, Section IV — narrative frame in the Ganguli translation witness
Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Nalopākhyāna, Sections LIII–LVII — Nala–Damayantī witness in the Ganguli translation
Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Pativratā-māhātmya, Sections CCXLI–CCXLII — Sāvitrī–Satyavān witness in the Ganguli translation
Oxford Bibliographies in Hinduism: Pamela Lothspeich, “Mahābhārata in Hindu Tradition,” and Simon Brodbeck, “Mahābhārata”
BORI official Critical Edition overview, used only to distinguish SRC-277
coverage_rule: Include six named individuals needed to make the umbrella scope legible without duplicating SRC-277’s large BORI cast or SRC-278’s Gītā dialogue: Ugraśravas Sauti and Śaunaka for the Sanskrit textual recital frame; Nala and Damayantī for the Nalopākhyāna; and Sāvitrī and Satyavān for the Pativratā-māhātmya. These are not an attempt at a comprehensive epic dramatis personae, a cross-tradition identity ledger, or a claim that these stories carry the same authority, form, or meaning in every living, regional, devotional, or performance context.
omissions: The 49-character BORI Critical Edition cohort in SRC-277, including its principal Kuru-war cast, and the four-character Bhagavad Gītā cohort in SRC-278. The same names, where they appear elsewhere, must never be identity-merged or claim-transferred across source IDs.

All other Sanskrit Mahābhārata figures, including hundreds of genealogy, war, pilgrimage, didactic, divine, rākṣasa, nāga, and embedded-tale figures; collective categories and unindividualized figures remain terms/context.

Regional recensions; vernacular retellings; oral, sung, ritual, theatrical, dance, visual, television, film, comic, game, and other performance/adaptation traditions; commentarial, sectarian, and devotional layers; South and Southeast Asian traditions not represented by these witnesses.
Harivaṃśa and other associated texts; any single manuscript, printed Sanskrit edition, or critical edition beyond the narrow boundary statement; translations other than the declared Ganguli witness.

Claims about contemporary Hindu belief or practice; fixed pan-Indian caste/varna, gender, sexuality, disability, ethnicity, race, political, legal, historical, or moral norms; and colonial-era translation language as a transparent substitute for Sanskrit categories.
uncertainties: Oxford scholarship describes the Mahābhārata as a narrative tradition with oral, textual, and performative versions. Accordingly, this pass does not treat a single printed text, translation, or critical edition as the whole tradition or as normatively superior.

Ganguli’s nineteenth-century English translation is a valuable accessible translation witness, but its Victorian diction, transliteration, selection, and section labels are not Sanskrit text, not a BORI Critical Edition translation, and not neutral language for caste, gender, sacred, or social categories. All Ganguli locators are marked as translation-witness locators only.

The BORI Critical Edition is intentionally separate in SRC-277. Its critical constitution, manuscript method, and character records cannot establish the content of this umbrella pass, and this umbrella cannot settle textual-critical questions or make a ‘most authentic’ claim.
The Bhagavad Gītā is an embedded, separately scoped sacred dialogue in SRC-278; its characters and terms are not re-recorded here merely because it occurs inside the epic.

Nala–Damayantī and Sāvitrī–Satyavān are selected only as bounded Sanskrit embedded narratives. Their later devotional, gendered, regional, performance, translation, and modern political receptions require their own witnesses and specialists.

Sanskrit terms remain source-native and context-dependent. Deva, asura, rākṣasa, nāga, dharma, karma, tapas, mantra, astra, vrata, varṇa, boon, curse, and kinship practices must not be flattened into D&D-style races, classes, alignments, mechanics, or universal social categories.
evidence_basis: The declared Ganguli translation supplies precise narrative section locators for the six selected figures and their three limited relationships. Oxford Academic supplies the scholarly rationale for a tradition-level, plural rather than single-text approach and notes the frame, eighteen-parvan structure, and subsidiary-tale breadth. BORI’s official page is cited only to enforce separation from SRC-277. No Wikipedia, fan source, unexamined vernacular adaptation, or claim about living practice is used as evidence.
